channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: The effectiveness of meaning-based interventions in reducing suicide-related vulnerability: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether meaning-based interventions (e.g., meaning-centered therapy, dignity therapy) reduce suicide-related vulnerability (ideation, hopelessness, demoralization) and how any benefits are mediated. Ten heterogeneous studies (7 RCTs, 2 quasi-experimental, 1 secondary analysis) were synthesized narratively.
FINDINGS: Across studies, meaning-based interventions consistently improved existential outcomes (meaning in life, spiritual well-being, quality of life) with moderate effect sizes. Emotional outcomes showed mixed and smaller effects. Suicide-related outcomes (hopelessness, demoralization, suicidal ideation) generally decreased, but results varied by population and intervention; no pooled effect sizes were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, methodologically mixed, and lacks meta-analytic pooling, limiting certainty. Most studies were at moderate risk of bias; heterogeneity in populations (e.g., advanced cancer, veterans, general psychiatric outpatients) and interventions precludes firm conclusions. The pattern suggests potential benefit via existential pathways, but causal mediation remains unproven. Larger, preregistered RCTs with standardized outcomes and mediation analyses are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify wholesale adoption of meaning-based interventions for suicide prevention outside research settings. Clinicians may consider adjunctive meaning-centered approaches for patients with existential distress, while monitoring suicide-related outcomes closely and integrating with evidence-based treatments.

item.title: Vitamin D Supplementation and Improvement in Insomnia Symptoms Among Malaysian Women With Vitamin D Deficiency: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common and disabling, and low vitamin D levels may contribute to sleep disturbance, especially in women. This is a double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (RCT) protocol testing weekly high-dose vitamin D₃ (50 000 IU) versus placebo for 9 weeks in Malaysian women aged 19–50 years with serum 25(OH)D <20 ng/mL and insomnia symptoms.
FINDINGS: Recruitment began December 2023; by July 2026, 42 were screened, 33 enrolled, 22 completed, 4 were still receiving intervention, and 1 withdrew. No efficacy results are yet available because the trial is ongoing and unblinded.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed RCT protocol with clear allocation concealment and validated sleep measures, but no outcome data are available to judge efficacy. The small sample size and single-centre, community-based setting limit generalisability. Until results are published, any claim of benefit remains speculative.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine vitamin D supplementation for insomnia. Clinicians should await trial results before considering vitamin D as adjunctive therapy; CBT remains first-line.

item.title: Characterizing Behavioral Engagement in Smartphone Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This secondary analysis of a 12-week RCT (N=60) examined behavioral engagement in smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for OCD using 21 objective app analytics variables. It aimed to characterize engagement profiles, link them to OCD symptom change, and explore associations with pretreatment credibility/expectancy and posttreatment satisfaction.
FINDINGS: Cluster analysis identified three engagement profiles: high (35%), moderate (52%), and low (13%) users. All clusters showed significant pre- to posttreatment reductions in OCD severity (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale), with no significant differences in symptom change across clusters. Cluster 3 (low users) reported lower treatment credibility, expectancy, and satisfaction than cluster 2, while app quality ratings were similar across clusters.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility of multidimensional engagement measurement in digital CBT, but the lack of differential symptom improvement across engagement profiles challenges simplistic dose-response assumptions. The findings may reflect true equivalence in effectiveness across engagement levels or be limited by small sample size and insufficient power to detect meaningful differences. Pretreatment expectations appear linked to engagement patterns, suggesting a modifiable target for improving adherence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results imply that even low engagement with smartphone CBT for OCD may yield clinical benefit, though expectations may influence engagement and satisfaction. Clinicians should consider addressing pretreatment expectations to enhance participation, but should not assume higher engagement necessarily leads to better outcomes.

item.title: Efficacy of Saffron as an Adjunct to Methylphenidate in Treating ADHD in Children Aged 6-12: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This 6-week randomized clinical trial (RCT) in children aged 6–12 with ADHD tested whether adding saffron extract to methylphenidate improves ADHD symptoms and working memory compared with methylphenidate alone.
FINDINGS: Of 58 randomized children, 43 completed the trial (22 in the combination group, 21 controls). Parent-reported total ADHD scores improved more with saffron+methylphenidate (p = 0.002, Cohen’s d = 0.85), as did hyperactivity (p = 0.024, d = 0.62), impulsivity (p = 0.031, d = 0.58), and attention (p = 0.001, d = 0.92). Objective measures (CPT) showed no significant group differences in impulsivity or inattention, though reaction time improved (p = 0.023, d = 0.45). Working memory (Corsi Block Span) did not differ between groups. No severe adverse effects were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests subjective symptom improvement with adjunctive saffron, but effects on objective cognitive measures are limited or absent. The small sample, short duration, and lack of placebo control limit internal validity; the large effect sizes on parent ratings may reflect expectation bias. Safety data are reassuring but preliminary.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of saffron as adjunct to methylphenidate for ADHD; larger, longer, placebo-controlled trials are needed to confirm any benefit and assess long-term safety.

item.title: Mortality Among People With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with increased all-cause and cause-specific mortality and whether ADHD medication modifies this risk. The study included 19 observational studies with over 15 million participants.
FINDINGS: ADHD was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.31–2.24), suicide (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.21–2.95), unintentional or intentional injury (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.22–2.00), and natural-cause mortality (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.16–1.38). Among individuals with ADHD, medication use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.64–0.87). Substantial heterogeneity was reported across studies.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests ADHD is linked to higher mortality across multiple causes, with medication associated with reduced risk. However, the observational nature of included studies, substantial heterogeneity, and potential confounding limit causal inference. The association between medication and reduced mortality may reflect confounding by indication or severity rather than a direct causal protective effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support timely diagnosis and treatment of ADHD, particularly given the elevated mortality risk. Clinicians should remain vigilant about suicide risk and injury prevention in this population, while recognizing that the protective effect of medication requires further confirmation in robust study designs.

item.title: Concentrated Exposure Therapy vs Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-center randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the efficacy of a concentrated 4-day exposure-based intervention (Bergen 4-day treatment, B4DT) with an 8-week unguided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) for adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), assessing outcomes over 3 months.
FINDINGS: 119 adults (mean age 33.5 years, 66.4% women) were randomized to B4DT (n=60) or iCBT (n=59). At posttreatment, B4DT showed a significantly greater reduction in OCD symptoms (Y-BOCS) than iCBT (mean difference -7.9 points, 95% CI -9.7 to -6.0; Hedges g = -1.6). At 3-month follow-up, the difference remained significant but smaller (mean difference -5.6 points, 95% CI -7.8 to -3.4; Hedges g = -1.0). Response and remission rates at follow-up were higher with B4DT (61.4% vs 25.0% and 42.1% vs 13.6%, respectively).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides high-quality RCT evidence that B4DT is superior to unguided iCBT for OCD symptom reduction, with large effect sizes at posttreatment and moderate effects sustained at 3 months. Strengths include masked outcome assessment, intention-to-treat analysis, and clear superiority in both primary and secondary outcomes. However, the single-center design, predominantly female sample, and lack of active iCBT comparator (e.g., therapist-guided) limit generalizability. The concentrated format may improve access but requires replication in diverse settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: B4DT may offer a more effective and time-efficient alternative to unguided iCBT for OCD, particularly where rapid symptom reduction is prioritized. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and logistical constraints when choosing between formats, while awaiting broader validation.

item.title: Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation With Gamified Cognitive Control Training for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, double-masked randomized clinical trial (RCT) evaluated the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with gamified cognitive control training (CCT) versus sham tDCS plus sham game in adults (18–65 years) with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addressed whether this combined home-based approach could improve depressive symptoms more than sham treatment.
FINDINGS: Of 111 enrolled participants, 109 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (55 active, 54 sham). Feasibility was met, with 78.9% (lower bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 71.5%) completing ≥20 of 30 sessions. Both groups showed MADRS score improvements at week 6, with no significant difference between groups (difference: 0.89 [95% CI, -1.37 to 3.15]; P = .44; Cohen d = 0.10 [95% CI, -0.15 to 0.34]). Results were consistent at week 10 follow-up. Adverse events were balanced between groups.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates that home-based tDCS with CCT is feasible and safe, but it does not show superior efficacy to sham treatment for reducing depressive symptoms in MDD. The small effect size (Cohen d = 0.10) suggests no clinically meaningful difference. Limitations include the lack of an active comparator (e.g., standard tDCS alone) and potential expectancy effects despite masking checks. The population was relatively young and predominantly female, which may limit generalizability. Further research is needed to optimize the combination of tDCS and behavioral interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support the use of home-based tDCS combined with gamified CCT as a superior treatment for MDD over sham. Clinicians should remain cautious about adopting this approach until more robust evidence emerges. Further trials should explore optimal stimulation parameters and cognitive interventions.

item.title: Assessing the Impact of Metacognitive Therapy on OCD Severity and Beliefs: A Three-Wave Multisite RCT With Panel Mediation Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This assessor-blinded multisite RCT (n=76 adults with OCD in Pakistan) tested whether 12 weekly sessions of individual metacognitive therapy (MCT) reduce OCD severity more than treatment-as-usual (TAU) and whether changes in metacognitive beliefs temporally precede symptom improvement.
FINDINGS: MCT produced greater reductions in clinician-rated Y-BOCS severity than TAU (F(1.81, 134)=11.30, p<0.001), with mean differences of −4.00 at post-treatment and −6.92 at 6-month follow-up (both p<0.001). MCT also reduced Metacognitions Questionnaire-30 belief domains, maintained at follow-up. However, the prespecified lagged indirect effect through post-treatment beliefs was not supported (β=−0.01).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows MCT outperforms TAU for OCD severity with moderate-to-large effects at post-treatment and follow-up, supporting external validity in a non-Western outpatient setting. However, the lack of temporal precedence in the mediation analysis weakens claims that metacognitive belief change is a causal mechanism. Limitations include small sample size, single-blind assessment, and absence of active comparator (e.g., ERP), leaving uncertainty about MCT’s superiority to established treatments. Funding sources are not reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MCT may be a viable alternative where ERP is declined or unavailable, but clinicians should note that the mechanism remains unclear and comparative effectiveness against first-line treatments is untested.

item.title: Structural network alterations and peripheral immune-inflammatory dysregulation define distinct subtypes of major depressive disorder with prognostic implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated whether immune-inflammatory dysregulation and cortical structural changes in major depressive disorder (MDD) interact systematically, and whether they define clinically meaningful subtypes. It combined genome-wide association data with a prospective cohort of 122 MDD patients and 66 healthy controls who underwent MRI and immune marker assessments.
FINDINGS: Genetically predicted MDD was linked to lower circulating IGF-1 (pFDR = 0.013). Higher IL-5 and leptin levels correlated with reduced gray matter volume in the right cingulate gyrus and bilateral putamen (pFDR < 0.05). Structural covariance network analysis identified two subtypes: hypoconnectivity (n = 49) with greater anxiety and anhedonia, and hyperconnectivity (n = 73) with elevated inflammatory markers and faster antidepressant response (p = 0.032).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence for immune-brain interaction in MDD and suggests two neurobiological subtypes with distinct symptom profiles and treatment responses. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is short, and causality cannot be inferred from associations. The clinical relevance of subtype-specific immune markers and the stability of subtypes over time remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet justify subtype-specific treatment choices but suggest that immune profiling and network connectivity measures might eventually help personalize MDD care. Further validation in larger, longer studies is needed before bedside application.

item.title: Greater proximity to greenspace is associated with fewer depressive symptoms among urban middle-aged adults.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study used machine-learning (Support Vector Machines) to rank predictors of depressive symptoms among 1,542 urban middle-aged adults in China, asking whether residential greenspace proximity matters more than other health and social factors.
FINDINGS: The best-performing model (AUC 0.776) identified life satisfaction, greenspace (EVI250 m), social activity, pain, sleep duration and instrumental-ADL impairment as significant predictors. Closer greenspace exposure was associated with fewer depressive symptoms; Shapley values placed greenspace among the top influential factors.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on satellite-derived greenspace metrics rather than direct environmental measurements. The ML approach improves variable ranking but cannot establish causality or rule out residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured neighbourhood or lifestyle factors). The reported AUC suggests moderate predictive power, but effect sizes for greenspace proximity are not provided, so clinical significance remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that urban greenspace may be a relevant—but likely modest—contributor to mental health; they do not yet justify changing practice, but they support further longitudinal and interventional research.

item.title: Symptom Trajectories and Attendance in Face-to-Face and Online Psychiatric Follow-Up for Major Depressive Disorder and Anxiety Symptoms: Prospective Observational Cohort Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, and access to specialist psychiatric follow-up remains limited in many settings. Telepsychiatry may reduce logistical barriers to care, but data on video-based follow-up under routine outpatient conditions in Türkiye are scarce, and comparisons of delivery modalities are frequently limited by baseline imbalance between self-selected groups.

item.title: Initial Treatment for Acute Low Back Pain and Risk of Opioid Use Disorder and Overdose.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Guideline-discordant care for acute low back pain (aLBP) is common and has been associated with adverse outcomes. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the incidence of new opioid use disorder (OUD) or overdose diagnosis among opioid-naive patients with Medicaid coverage initiating treatment for aLBP and to evaluate the association between initial treatment modalities and subsequent risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis.

item.title: Treatment provided for Danish adolescents who attempt suicide.
item.description: PURPOSE: After a suicide attempt, adolescents should ideally receive psychosocial assessment and aftercare. We investigated the proportion of girls and boys receiving mental health treatment and social interventions within the first weeks and one year after a suicide attempt. METHODS: This study included a national cohort of children born in Denmark in 1996-2003 who had a hospital-recorded suicide attempt before age 18 years (N = 3650).

item.title: Neural correlates of self-directed violence: A large-sample resting-state fMRI study from UK Biobank.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Suicide remains a leading cause of death worldwide, underscoring the importance of identifying neurobiological markers associated with suicidal behaviors. While nonsuicidal self-directed violence (NSSDV) is an established risk factor for future suicide attempts (SAs), the underlying neural distinctions between these behaviors remain insufficiently understood. METHODS: A total of 1,070 participants with a history of self-directed violence (SDV) were stratified into SA (n = 579) and NSSDV (n = 491) groups based on self-reported questionnaires.

item.title: Neural dysfunction underlying divergent thinking and its shared mechanisms with protracted withdrawal symptoms in heroin use disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Drug use may induce transient bursts of inspiration but is also associated with increasing cognitive rigidity. How neurological damage induced by drug addiction affects higher-order thinking processes in humans remains elusive. This gap limits our understanding of broader cognitive impairment in addiction and prolonged maladaptation during withdrawal. METHODS: The study investigated divergent thinking, a key component of flexible behavior, in heroin use disorder (HUD). Behavioral performance was assessed using the Realistic Presented Problem-Solving Task.

item.title: 'What doesn't kill you doesn't always make you stronger': The impact of repeated exposure to adverse life events on mental health.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Repeated exposure to adversity is universal to the human experience and may impact mental health negatively. However, competing hypotheses predict that repeated adversity leads to either sensitisation or habituation. METHODS: Using a 22-year Australian population-based panel study, we examined changes in mental health following repeated exposure to seven common adverse life events in adulthood. Mixed-effects regression models estimated the relationship between repeated exposure to adverse life events of the same type and its impact on the Mental Health Inventory-5 score.

item.title: Alcohol reinforcers attenuate goal-directed control in individuals with and without alcohol use disorder.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Impaired control over alcohol consumption is a core feature of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet its mechanisms remain unclear. Habit theories posit a shift from goal-directed to habitual control with repeated alcohol use, but human evidence is mixed and often lacks translational alignment with animal models. Recent accounts therefore call for paradigms assessing contingency sensitivity with disorder-relevant reinforcers.

item.title: Mapping emotional contagion: directional predictive patterns of depressive symptoms among middle-aged and older Chinese couples.
item.description: BACKGROUND: China's aging population faces increased prevalence in mid- and later life depression, with married middle-aged and older women vulnerable due to disproportionate caregiving and socioeconomic stress. Although emotional contagion between partners is well-documented, pathways through which depressive symptoms spread between these spouses remain unclear. This study examines the directional predictive patterns of depressive symptoms, wives to husbands specifically, within middle-aged and older Chinese couples.

item.title: Green-synthesized Nanoparticles as Emerging Antidepressant and Anxiolytic Candidates: A Critical Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Prospects.
item.description: The high incidence of depression and anxiety disorders worldwide, with figures of depression > 300 million and anxiety > 264 million, poses a serious challenge to health and wellness. Treatment is still limited by existing pharmacotherapies with delayed onset, adverse side effects, poor entry into the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and resistance in approximately 30% of patients. Green-synthesized nanoparticles (NPs) obtained via phytochemicals, microorganisms, and biomolecules are a promising sustainable route for neurotherapeutic applications.

item.title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols.

item.title: [Training teams in suicide risk assessment: the role of advanced practice nurses].
item.description: Suicide risk encompasses a variety of complex clinical situations that require specific skills on the part of nurses. A process of reflecting on past experiences provides a better understanding of the role of advanced practice nurses in their interdisciplinary collaboration and clinical leadership responsibilities. The implementation of a training program on suicide risk prevention at a medical-psychological center concretely illustrates their contribution to enhancing team competencies.

item.title: Psychoplastogens to Reduce Persistent Cognitive Symptoms for Traumatic Brain Injury as a Chronic Condition.
item.description: There are currently no available effective pharmacological therapies for treating chronic cognitive deficits after traumatic brain injury (TBI). Psychoplastogens, including atypical psychedelics, classical serotonergic psychedelics, and neuroplastogens, are a class of small molecule drugs that can enhance neuroplasticity by inducing rapid and sustained effects on neuronal architecture and function, with the potential to have broad therapeutic effects.

item.title: Formative Assessment of Factors Influencing Implementation of Alcohol Screening and Brief Intervention for HIV Outpatient Services in Viet Nam.
item.description: BackgroundAlcohol screening and brief intervention (SBI) is not routinely integrated into HIV outpatient care in Viet Nam. This study aimed to identify anticipated barriers and facilitators at the pre-implementation stage of alcohol SBI intervention in a HIV outpatient clinic (OPC) in Viet Nam.MethodsWe conducted a qualitative formative assessment guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR).

item.title: [Risk factors associated with post-partum depression in first-time mothers].
item.description: Being a first-time mother is a new transition for a woman, and she must adapt to various physiological, psychological and relational factors that interact with one another. The transition can make the woman more emotionally vulnerable and at an increased risk of developing post-partum depression (PPD). This review is based on a systematic literature search and presents several risk factors associated with PPD in primiparous women. Hopefully, knowledge about risk factors can help identify women who might be at risk to ensure that early interventions can be initiated and thereby prevent PPD.

item.title: Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing in trauma related panic disorder: clinical outcomes through a neuroendocrine lens.
item.description: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy on symptoms and disease severity in individuals diagnosed with panic disorders who had experienced at least 1 traumatic event. METHODS: This study was conducted using a single-group pretest posttest experimental design. Participants received the standard EMDR protocol, and symptom severity was assessed using the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) at 4 separate time points (pretreatment, post-first session, post-second session, and posttreatment).

item.title: [Opioid substitution and pain management in a case of severe PTSD].
item.description: This case report describes a highly complicated case with combined chronic pain, substance use disorder (SUD) and social challenges following war participation in Ukraine. The patient had developed PTSD and SUD because of pain management and was enrolled in dual diagnosis treatment in out-patient psychiatry. The patient successfully transitioned to long-acting buprenorphine leading to better pain management and remission in SUD, improving both treatment relation and clinical treatment of PTSD by use of integrated dual diagnosis treatment.

item.title: Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer for multimodal EEG-fMRI learning in ADHD diagnosis.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with distributed alterations in large-scale brain systems, making reliable diagnosis from neuroimaging data challenging. EEG-derived and fMRI-derived static functional-connectivity profiles summarize patterns of electrophysiological coupling and hemodynamic covariation, respectively, but their heterogeneous signal mechanisms make direct multimodal alignment difficult. NEW METHOD: We propose a Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer (CM-MCT) for EEG-fMRI based ADHD diagnosis.

item.title: Paternal methylphenidate exposure alters sperm miRNAs and induces intergenerational behavioral and transcriptional changes that are largely reversed by washout.
item.description: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Methylphenidate (MPH), a first-line medication, is often used long-term and not routinely discontinued in individuals planning to have children. Guided by the Paternal Origins of Health and Disease framework, in this study, we investigated intergenerational effects of paternal MPH exposure and reversibility of sperm epigenetic changes.

item.title: Population-Based Rates of Youth Suicide-Related Emergency Department Encounters by Rural-Urban Status.
item.description: PURPOSE: To compare population-based rates and mechanisms of suicide-related emergency department (ED) encounters among rural and urban youth in Kentucky and Arkansas. METHODS: We conducted a population-based cross-sectional study using 2018-2021 Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project State Emergency Department Databases linked with U.S. Census population estimates. Suicide-related ED encounters among youth aged 10-19 years were identified using diagnosis codes for suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and intentional self-harm.

item.title: The Developmental Profile Inventory: Factor Structure and Preliminary Convergent Validity Evidence in a Norwegian Sample.
item.description: We examined the factor structure and convergent validity of the Developmental Profile Inventory (DPI), a self-report assessing psychodynamic personality functioning. The DPI is based on the Developmental Profile model, which integrates psychodynamic theories into a hierarchical developmental framework conceptualizing personality functioning in nine adaptive and maladaptive developmental levels. Each level comprises the following three domains: self, interpersonal functioning, and problem-solving strategies.

item.title: "A Literal Form of Torture" - Health Care Stakeholder Perspectives on Sleep and Wellbeing Among First-Time Parents in Ireland During the Postpartum Period.
item.description: PURPOSE: Postpartum sleep loss and fatigue are common during the transition to parenthood, with important implications for parental health and wellbeing. Given their role in supporting families during this transition, health care stakeholders can provide valuable insight into the sleep-related challenges experienced by first-time parents. DESIGN: This study employed a narrative inquiry approach to examine health care stakeholders' (e.g. midwives, psychologists, and doulas) perceptions, attitudes, and opinions regarding sleep and wellbeing among first-time parents during the postpartum period.

item.title: Dual benefit of esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia on postoperative pain and mental health outcomes in patients undergoing bariatric surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated whether esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) improves postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes in morbidly obese patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, compared to conventional opioid-based anesthesia.
FINDINGS: 84 patients were randomized (1:1) to esketamine-based OFA (n=42) or opioid-based anesthesia with remifentanil (n=42). 74 (88.1%) completed 3-month follow-up. Postoperative pain intensity within 24 hours was significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.01), with fewer patients experiencing moderate-to-severe pain (P < 0.05). At 3 months, mental health outcomes were significantly better in the esketamine group. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Pharmacokinetic analysis confirmed rapid esketamine metabolism to active (S)-norketamine.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests esketamine-based OFA may offer dual benefits for acute pain and longer-term mental health without increasing adverse events. Strengths include the double-blind RCT design, clear co-primary outcomes, and pharmacokinetic confirmation. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is limited to 3 months, and the mental health assessment tools are not specified. The lack of blinding details for outcome assessors and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline mental health severity) limit certainty. The clinical significance of the observed mental health improvement remains uncertain given the short follow-up and unspecified measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine-based OFA may be a promising alternative to opioid-based anesthesia in bariatric surgery, potentially improving immediate postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes. However, larger trials with longer follow-up and validated mental health measures are needed before recommending a change in practice.

item.title: Impact of clozapine on the proteome: A systematic review and functional analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), but its use is limited by serious adverse effects. This systematic review and functional proteomic analysis aimed to integrate proteomic findings associated with clozapine exposure across animal, human, and cell-based models to better understand its mechanisms and potential biomarkers.
FINDINGS: Across 1070 unique proteins altered by clozapine (603 increased, 394 decreased, 73 discordant), 152 were identified in ≥2 studies, with 79 showing concordant directionality. Nine proteins were replicated in ≥3 studies. STRING pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in immune/inflammatory, cellular-stress, and neuronal pathways, with stratified analyses supporting these and related metabolic processes. IPA highlighted necrosis-related processes and downstream effects in cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal systems. No direct comparison of brain and peripheral blood changes was available.
INTERPRETATION: This systematic review provides preliminary evidence that clozapine may influence immune, inflammatory, and cell-death pathways, potentially contributing to adverse effects. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with limited replication of specific proteins and no direct clinical correlation to treatment response or adverse outcomes. The lack of longitudinal human data and time-series comparisons limits causal inference. The findings are hypothesis-generating and underscore the need for prospective proteomic studies during clozapine initiation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current proteomic data do not yet translate to clinical practice but suggest potential biomarkers for monitoring clozapine-related adverse effects. Clinicians should remain vigilant for immune-mediated complications (e.g., myocarditis) but should not alter prescribing based on these findings alone. Further research is needed to validate these pathways as therapeutic targets or biomarkers.

item.title: Extended-Release Guanfacine Hydrochloride is Safe and Effective as Mono- and Adjunctive Therapy in Children and Adolescents with ADHD: A Naturalistic, Multi-Center, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures-Based Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This naturalistic, multicenter, retrospective cohort study in Türkiye assessed the safety and effectiveness of extended-release guanfacine hydrochloride (GXR) as mono- or adjunctive therapy in 567 children and adolescents (mean age 11.2 years) with ADHD, including high rates of comorbidity (82.4%). The study used clinician-rated CGI scales and parent-reported symptom scales over a 6-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: GXR (median dose 2.0–3.0 mg/day) was associated with symptom improvement, with a low rate of adverse effects. Greater improvement was observed in hyperactive-impulsive (HI) symptoms than inattentive (IA) symptoms. Children with comorbid autism spectrum disorder (ASD; 30% of sample) also showed notable clinical improvement. Baseline symptom severity modified treatment response.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s naturalistic design and lack of a comparator group limit causal inference. The large sample size and real-world setting enhance external validity, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., concurrent therapies, clinician bias) may influence results. The differential effect on HI symptoms and effectiveness in ASD are hypothesis-generating but require confirmation in controlled trials. The low adverse effect rate aligns with prior safety data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GXR may be a reasonable option for ADHD in youth with comorbidities, particularly for hyperactivity-impulsivity or ASD, but clinicians should weigh its modest differential effects against alternatives. Further randomized evidence is needed to guide treatment selection.

item.title: Harm reduction among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO-registered) examined harm reduction policies and services for substance use among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon, a setting with high refugee density and complex legal/healthcare barriers. The review aimed to map service availability, access barriers, and policy gaps to guide interventions.
FINDINGS: Out of 387 records, 29 documents (17 peer-reviewed studies and 12 grey literature reports) were included. No structured harm reduction policies specifically for refugees were identified. Key barriers included legal restrictions, stigma, and poor integration of harm reduction into routine care. Only 4 of 12 grey literature sources mentioned harm reduction provision, and none outlined a comprehensive strategy. Many studies were broad and lacked focused substance-use data in refugee populations.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak and fragmented, with high risk of selection and reporting biases due to reliance on grey literature and heterogeneous, often non-refugee-specific studies. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used for risk-of-bias assessment, but the overall quality of included evidence appears low. The lack of policy specificity and integrated services is clear, but causal pathways and effect sizes remain unquantified. Further targeted research is essential to inform policy adaptation and service design.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current harm reduction services in Lebanon do not adequately address refugee needs; clinicians should anticipate gaps in access and advocate for mobile clinics and integrated HCV screening. However, evidence to guide specific clinical interventions is currently insufficient.

item.title: Brain functional changes of suicidal ideation and behaviours: a meta-analysis of task-based fMRI studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pre-registered meta-analysis of 22 task-based fMRI studies examined brain functional changes associated with suicidal ideation and behaviours, comparing 459 suicidal individuals with 681 non-suicidal psychiatric controls. The study aimed to clarify neural underpinnings of suicidality amid methodological heterogeneity.
FINDINGS: In emotion tasks, general suicidality and suicidal behaviours were linked to hyperactivity in the left sensorimotor cortices and hippocampus/parahippocampus, alongside hypoactivity in bilateral visual cortices. Only the visual cortex hypoactivity was consistently replicated across all subgroup analyses. In non-emotion tasks, hyperactivity in the left precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus was observed for general suicidality and suicidal behaviours, consistently replicated across subgroups. Meta-regression showed larger functional changes in frontotemporal regions with higher female proportions and in hippocampal/temporal regions with older participants.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to methodological heterogeneity across studies (e.g., varied diagnoses, task types). The consistent finding of visual cortex hypoactivity in emotion tasks and motor/temporal hyperactivity in non-emotion tasks suggests potential neural targets for intervention. However, the clinical significance of these neural changes remains uncertain, as effect sizes and direct clinical outcomes were not reported. The study’s reliance on task-based fMRI and subgroup analyses limits generalisability to routine psychiatric care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings highlight potential neural correlates of suicidality but do not yet translate into actionable clinical tools. Further research is needed to determine if these neural patterns can guide treatment or risk assessment in psychiatric practice.

item.title: Targeting affective cognition during pregnancy to prevent postpartum depression: a randomized controlled trial with parity-specific effects.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested whether prenatal affective cognitive training (PACT) reduces postpartum depression (PPD) risk in pregnant women at heightened risk by targeting negative cognitive biases related to infant cues. The study included 147 pregnant women identified as high-risk, randomized to PACT or care as usual (CAU), with outcomes assessed up to six months postpartum.
FINDINGS: The primary outcome, PPD incidence within six months postpartum, did not differ significantly between PACT (14%) and CAU (24%) overall (p = 0.18). Secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms over the first six weeks postpartum, also showed no significant difference (p = 0.31). However, PACT significantly improved positive interpretation of infant emotions post-intervention (p = 0.003). Exploratory analyses revealed a markedly lower PPD incidence in multiparous women receiving PACT (5%) compared to CAU (35%), with an odds ratio of 0.10 (95% CI [0.01-0.92], p = 0.04). Follow-up data were available for 83% of participants.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by its RCT design and structured intervention, but the lack of overall effect on PPD incidence limits conclusions. The significant improvement in affective cognition suggests the intervention may target relevant mechanisms, though clinical significance is unclear. The exploratory parity-specific findings are intriguing but require cautious interpretation due to small subgroup sizes and lack of correction for multiple testing. The high dropout-adjusted follow-up rate (83%) is a strength, but the study’s power may have been insufficient for subgroup analyses. External validity is limited by the selective high-risk population and single-center setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PACT does not currently reduce PPD risk overall, so it cannot be recommended for routine practice. However, the parity-specific effect in multiparous women warrants further investigation in larger, adequately powered trials to determine if targeted interventions could benefit specific subgroups. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting exploratory findings.

item.title: Structure based discovery of antipsychotic-like TAAR1 agonists.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study used computational docking and experimental screening to discover novel trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) agonists as potential antipsychotic agents in schizophrenia, where current dopamine/serotonin-targeting treatments have limited efficacy and side effects.
FINDINGS: From 65 million computationally screened molecules, 55 were experimentally tested, yielding 14 TAAR1 agonists with mid-nanomolar to micromolar potencies. Hit optimization produced nanomolar agonists, with three compounds demonstrating high brain exposure and potency comparable to or exceeding the investigational drug ulotaront. All three normalized amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice (a schizophrenia model) without inducing catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.
INTERPRETATION: This is a high-throughput, computational-experimental drug discovery study with strong internal validity in its methodology (docking, cryo-EM confirmation, behavioral assays). However, it is entirely preclinical, conducted in mice, and lacks human data. The functional selectivity and lack of catalepsy are promising, but clinical relevance remains uncertain until safety and efficacy are tested in humans. The risk of over-optimization for initial hit rates is noted but not quantified.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change to clinical practice is warranted. These findings justify further development and human trials but should not alter current antipsychotic prescribing.

item.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=196) tested whether a single subanesthetic dose of esketamine (0.2 mg/kg IV) reduces postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) on day 3 after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia in women.
FINDINGS: In intention-to-treat analysis, PSD incidence on POD 3 was 13.06% with esketamine vs 24.90% with placebo (risk difference −11.84 pp [95% CI −22.98 to −0.69]; RR 0.52 [95% CI 0.28–0.99]; P=0.047). Per-protocol results were similar. PSD on POD 1 did not differ. Postoperative pain at 30 min was lower with esketamine (P<0.001), but dreaming was more frequent (21.4% vs 11.2%; P=0.048) and recovery metrics were modestly longer (time to alertness 12 vs 11 min; PACU stay 34 vs 31 min; both P≤0.005).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest reduction in PSD at POD 3 with esketamine, but the effect size is small (RR ~0.5) and the confidence interval barely excludes the null. The trial is single-center, short-term, and lacks long-term sleep or functional outcomes. Recovery time and dreaming frequency are slightly increased. Overall certainty is low; confirmation in larger, multicenter studies with longer follow-up is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, esketamine cannot be recommended routinely to prevent PSD after oocyte retrieval; any benefit appears small and may be offset by longer recovery. Monitor for transient side effects and counsel patients accordingly.

item.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence on whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy improves outcomes in major depressive disorder (MDD), and under what conditions such benefits occur.
FINDINGS: The review reports that combined rTMS plus pharmacotherapy may accelerate early symptom improvement, increase response and remission rates, and reduce relapse risk compared with either modality alone. These effects are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains. Neuroimaging studies suggest treatment-associated changes in hippocampal volume and network connectivity, but causal links to clinical improvement remain unclear. Expectancy effects and limitations in sham blinding complicate interpretation of clinical benefits.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes diverse evidence rather than providing pooled effect sizes or definitive conclusions. Strengths include integration across mechanistic and clinical domains; limitations include lack of quantitative meta-analysis, potential selection and publication bias, and unresolved causal pathways. The clinical significance of any observed benefits remains uncertain without standardized effect estimates and rigorous RCT data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of combined rTMS and antidepressants outside research or highly specialized settings. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting heterogeneous findings and await more definitive trials before changing practice.

item.title: Health risks of alcohol consumption in Aotearoa New Zealand: modelling to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This modelling study estimated alcohol-attributable mortality in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ) to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines (LRDGs), using a multi-state life-table model with NZ-specific data and WHO/GBD relative risk (RR) libraries. The cohort consisted of 12-year-olds followed over their lifetime with fixed 2018 exposure and disease rates.
FINDINGS: Males reached a 1-in-100 risk of alcohol-attributable death at 8.6 standard drinks (10 g ethanol) per week [95% UI 3.1–12.0], while females reached this threshold at 9.2 standard drinks [95% UI 3.7–12.4] using WHO RR data. Removing GBD one-star evidence conditions reduced thresholds to 2.7 (males) and 3.5 (females) standard drinks per week. Māori reached risk thresholds at lower consumption levels than non-Māori.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights that current NZ LRDGs may underestimate alcohol-related harm, particularly when excluding low-certainty evidence. Strengths include the use of a validated life-table model and NZ-specific data; limitations include reliance on modelled RRs, fixed 2018 rates, and uncertainty intervals spanning large ranges. The clinical significance is uncertain until guideline committees formally review these thresholds and consider population-specific risks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current NZ low-risk guidelines may need revision, especially for Māori. Clinicians should continue to advise patients on alcohol-related risks while awaiting updated national guidance.

item.title: Clozapine, suicide prevention and risk perception in psychiatry.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This editorial discusses clozapine’s role in reducing suicide risk in treatment-resistant schizophrenia, while noting its underutilization despite evidence of benefit. It explores whether historical risk perception biases in psychiatry contribute to this paradox.
FINDINGS: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with consistent evidence for reducing suicidal behavior, including suicide attempts and completed suicides, in schizophrenia. However, its use is limited by concerns over agranulocytosis and other adverse effects, despite improved monitoring protocols.
INTERPRETATION: As an editorial, this is not a primary research study but a conceptual analysis. It highlights a potential bias in risk assessment—overemphasizing treatment-related mortality (e.g., agranulocytosis) while underweighting the mortality risk from untreated severe mental illness, particularly suicide. The argument is plausible but relies on narrative reasoning rather than empirical data. No effect sizes or statistical comparisons are provided.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The piece suggests that clinicians may be overly cautious about clozapine due to historical fears, potentially denying patients a life-saving treatment. It does not change practice directly but may encourage a re-evaluation of risk-benefit assessments in clozapine prescribing.

item.title: Classroom-based observation and intervention of executive function for special education teachers working with preschoolers with Autism.
item.description: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Executive function (EF) related behavioral challenges are frequently observed in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder. However, structured, classroom-based observation of these behaviors by teachers remains difficult, resulting in limited practical assessment and recommendations for classroom-based support. This study aimed to examine the feasibility of teacher-administered EF assessment in special education centers and to formulate preliminary, expert-informed recommendations for autistic children with varying communication abilities.

item.title: Preliminary Evaluation of Implementation and Effectiveness of the Relational Suicide Intervention Pilot.
item.description: Although primary interventions for suicidal ideation typically focus on individuals, couple-based clinical interventions for this population remain underdeveloped. Despite emerging evidence suggesting that relational interventions may improve suicidal ideation, currently only one couple-based intervention has preliminary evidence, and it was specifically designed for military couples. This gap highlights the need for systemic couple-based interventions in outpatient settings.

item.title: Advancing the use of artificial intelligence in psychiatry: The need for international collaboration.
item.description: Challenging macrotrends in recent decades have characterised population mental health across the globe, with apparent deterioration in adolescent mental health, as well as underfunded, inequitable, and inefficient psychiatric care systems [1]. Unnecessary delays to treatment are widespread, with systemic difficulties, such as clinician burnout, a dearth of funding, and staff shortages, negatively impacting mental health care across Europe and beyond [2]. With limited clinician time and resources available, new methods for improving mental health care are an urgent priority.

item.title: Medical assistance in dying on psychiatric versus somatic grounds: survey on the experiences of relatives.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Relatives are often intimately involved in medical assistance in dying (MAID) on both psychiatric and somatic grounds. Greater insight into the extent to which certain experiences occur in practice will help physicians provide support. AIMS: To investigate how relatives of patients who received psychiatric versus somatic MAID scored on measures of opinions and emotions regarding the MAID trajectory; involvement in the trajectory; and judgement of the due care criteria.

item.title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function.
item.description: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets.

item.title: Characterizing gradients of functional connectome underpinning rumination and their alteration in depression.
item.description: As a prominent psychopathological process of major depressive disorder (MDD), rumination's brain underpinnings remain unclear. Emerging studies have highlighted that the brain is organized along several macroscale gradients, which could serve as a powerful framework for better understanding how the functional connectome underlies rumination. In this study, we leveraged two datasets (Rum-Beijing and Rum-MDD) to characterize the gradient structure during an active ruminative state.

item.title: The paradox of high IQ in ADHD: dissociable effects on inattention and impulsivity - insights from behavior, cognition & brain in 5138 children.
item.description: While Intelligence Quotient (IQ) is widely considered a linear protective factor against attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), this paradigm fails to capture domain-specific nuances. We investigated whether non-linear relationships between IQ profiles and ADHD symptoms exist in a large cohort of children diagnosed with ADHD using a multidimensional dataset that integrates behavioral assessments, cognitive testing, and neuroimaging data.

item.title: Post-Diagnosis Depression and Suicide Risk Among Cancer Survivors: A Nationwide Population-Based Cohort Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Patients with cancer are at increased risk of suicide, but the contribution of depression arising after cancer diagnosis remains poorly characterised. AIMS: To evaluate whether first-recorded depression after cancer diagnosis was associated with subsequent suicide risk among adults with cancer who had no documented depression before cancer diagnosis. METHODS: Using the South Korean National Health Insurance Service database. 755,079 adults newly diagnosed with cancer between 2009 and 2013, without documented depression before cancer diagnosis, were followed through 2023.
